title: The True Nature of All Phenomena
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and it is also the watershed that divides the Buddhadharma from the teachings of outsiders and of Mara. The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says: "For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."

inline.s: The true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and it is also the watershed that divides the Buddhadharma from the teachings of outsiders and of Mara. The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says:

"For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."
Master Zhiyi's Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra says:

"As for the lesser-vehicle sutras, if they bear the seal of the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvana, then they are the Buddha's teaching, and one who cultivates them attains the Way; if they lack the three dharma seals, then they are Mara's teaching. A Mahayana sutra has only one dharma seal, namely the true nature of all phenomena; it is called a sutra of definitive meaning and can lead one to the great Way. If it lacks the seal of true reality, it is Mara's teaching."
(For a more detailed discussion of the true nature of all phenomena, see
Selected Annotations on the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha

Since ancient times, the philosophies of East and West alike have tirelessly sought the essence of the universe and all things. Yet Shakyamuni Buddha, more than two thousand years ago, already gave the correct answer:
The essence of the universe and all things is the true nature of all phenomena.
Looking at modern science, the Buddha's assertions are being confirmed one by one, which only makes the Buddha's great wisdom appear all the more ultimate and perfect.

blocks.text: 1. What Is the True Nature of All Phenomena

inline.s: The so-called "true reality" means the actual state of affairs; the "true nature of all phenomena" means the actual state of affairs of all phenomena. The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha says:
"What is called the true nature of all phenomena? It is that all phenomena are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever."
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says:
"All phenomena are like illusions; the Tathagata, amid them, by the power of skillful means, is stained by nothing."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"The great bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as empty, as true reality, neither inverted nor moving, neither retreating nor turning."

[Dharma] In Buddhist studies, "dharma" has several meanings: 1. It refers to things and phenomena, including both the material and the mental; 2. Law, principle, regularity; 3. The way of cultivation, that is, the principles, methods, and states of cultivating the Way; 4. It is synonymous with "the Way." 5. The mental objects among the six dusts (forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental objects). Which meaning is intended must be judged from the context. The "dharma" in "the true nature of all phenomena" refers to things and phenomena. [All phenomena] refers to the myriad things and phenomena, all that is arrayed before us.
[Emptiness] Having appearance but no substantial reality (like things in a dream) is called "emptiness." In the Sutra of Holding the World,
Chapter Three on the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha says:
"Knowing that all phenomena are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root."

When describing the existence of things, besides "existent" and "nonexistent" there is another case, namely illusion, such as things in a dream, which do not truly exist but have appearance without substantial reality; the concept of "emptiness" is used to describe this. Master Hanshan says:
"The Buddha spoke the word 'emptiness' to break people's attachment to things as truly existent, not to mean absolute nothingness or annihilation."
The Vimalakirti Sutra,
Chapter Three on the Disciples, says:
"All phenomena are ultimately without anything whatsoever; this is the meaning of emptiness."

In this passage, "all phenomena" means that appearances exist, and "ultimately without anything whatsoever" means that in reality there is nothing (ultimately, there is nothing at all). This state in which appearances exist but reality does not (illusion) is called emptiness. Master Hanshan gave a profound exposition of "emptiness is precisely illusion; illusion means that which exists but is not real," which is excerpted below:
"Your letter seeking instruction is most sincere. Yet you have not grasped the two words 'emptiness' and 'illusion' correctly
(accurately)

, and so you are not without obstruction regarding mind and objects, which is why your practice is hard to carry out. Now I will explain it clearly for you, and then you will understand with no further doubt. The so-called 'emptiness' is not the emptiness of absolute nothingness; it is just as the common saying goes, 'as if no one were beside him' -- is it really true that no one is beside him? It is merely that
(simply)

he holds his head high and does not count that person in his eyes. The so-called 'illusion' is not the illusion of weird transformations; it means that which exists but is not real. It is like a peep-show box in the marketplace, out of which many figures are produced. Yet within that box there is originally nothing at all, and yet suddenly there they are; though they exist, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are fundamentally nonexistent, and because they are fundamentally nonexistent, we speak of emptiness. Hence it is said: 'Like an illusory man -- it is not that there is no illusory man, but the illusory man is not a real man.' If a person is not real, is that not emptiness? The Buddha spoke the word 'emptiness' to break people's attachment to things as truly existent, not to mean absolute nothingness or annihilation. Fearing that people might fall into annihilationism, he further spoke the word 'illusion' to dispel that view of annihilation. Thus all phenomena of body and mind are empty because they are illusory, and because they are empty they are said to be like illusions."
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Instruction to Zhou Ziyin)

[Peep-show box] A wooden box containing rolled-up pictures, with a row of small round holes on top (three or four holes), each fitted with a magnifying lens. After customers pay, they all put their eyes close to the holes and look inside. The box owner then slowly turns the handle on the side of the box, and so one picture after another passes continuously before the viewer's eyes. Usually the pictures depict stories one after another.
From this we can know that emptiness and illusion are synonyms. The Heart Sutra says:

"When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva was practicing the profound prajnaparamita, he illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they were all empty, and thus passed beyond all suffering and distress. Shariputra! Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form. The same is true of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra,
Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion, says:

"Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. ... Form is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form. World-Honored One, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness."
Comparing these two passages of scripture carefully, one knows that "emptiness" means precisely "illusion."

The true nature of all phenomena is the most ultimate truth, and so it is called the supreme meaning. Yet just as Copernicus declared in his day that the earth revolves around the sun rather than the sun around the earth, and people simply could not believe it -- Bruno was even judged a heretic and burned to death for proclaiming this truth -- so too the World-Honored One, in the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha,

Chapter One on the True Nature of All Phenomena, gave ten similes in succession to show how difficult it is for people to believe and understand the truth of the true nature of all phenomena. For example, one of the similes:
"Shariputra, suppose a person chews and swallows Mount Sumeru
(Mount Sumeru)

and can consume it entirely, and flies through space without harm -- what do you think, is this rare? It is rare, World-Honored One! Shariputra, that all phenomena spoken by all Buddhas are unborn, unceasing, signless, and unconditioned, and that people believe and understand this, is far more rare."
Though it is hard to believe and understand, the true nature of all phenomena is the truth, the supreme and unsurpassable truth. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:
"The foremost, rarest, and most difficult to understand Dharma attained by the Buddha -- only a Buddha together with a Buddha can fully fathom the true nature of all phenomena."

Therefore, if one tries to investigate and ponder the true nature of all phenomena with an ordinary person's wisdom, it is like a firefly burning Mount Sumeru: it can never set it alight. So the Buddha's disciples need only believe and accept the Buddha's words and practice according to the teaching!
Question: What is the nature of phenomena?

Answer: The nature of phenomena is the essential nature (essence) of all phenomena; it is another name for the true nature of all phenomena. The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit says:

"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person in a night dream sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
he sees nothing at all."
The Great Jewel Heap Sutra,
Volume Sixty-Four, says:
"Neither coming nor going, nor arising -- the Buddha can expound such a Dharma; though he says the essence of all phenomena is empty, the World Hero still causes them to cultivate the path."
The Moon Lamp Samadhi Sutra says:

"The essence of all phenomena is ever quiescent; ordinary people, lacking wisdom, cannot realize it. If one can settle the mind in quiescent concentration, that person always has the Buddha with him."
The Avatamsaka Sutra,
Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru, says:
"The nature of phenomena is originally empty and quiescent, neither grasped nor seen."
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"Living beings and lands share one nature of phenomena."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
"The nature of phenomena is as previously explained: each phenomenon is empty, and they are all one emptiness; this is the nature of phenomena."
[World Hero] Another name for the Buddha.
Question: Since the nature of phenomena is empty, doing good and doing evil should make no difference. Why then should one still observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds so diligently?

Answer: Ultimately speaking, doing good and doing evil make no difference, because both are matters within the dream of ignorance and are equally empty. But we are still within the dream of ignorance, and there doing good and doing evil differ greatly; we are governed by the law of cause and effect, good deeds bring good rewards and evil deeds bring evil rewards, and joy and sorrow are vividly clear, as if real. Our observance of precepts and cultivation is precisely for the sake of awakening, for removing delusion and inversion, and for waking from this delusive dream.
Question: What is the dharma realm?

Answer: As to the aspect of things, "dharma" means phenomena and "realm" means division: all things in the phenomenal realm each have their own distinct and different characteristics and cannot be confused with one another, which is called the "realm of phenomena." As to the aspect of principle, although phenomena are infinitely varied in appearance, they share one and the same nature, which is called the "realm of principle," that is, the true nature of all phenomena.
Question: What is the one true dharma realm?
Answer: The one true dharma realm is the term used by the Huayan school for the most ultimate principle, just as the Tiantai school speaks of the true nature of all phenomena.
Question: What is meant by dependent origination and emptiness of nature?

Answer: Dependent origination means that all phenomena arise from the convergence of many conditions; this is spoken from the aspect of things. Emptiness of nature means that all phenomena are inherently empty in nature and do not truly exist; this is spoken from the aspect of principle.

blocks.text: 2. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the Fundamental Principle of the Buddhadharma

inline.s: The one great matter for which the Buddha appeared in the world was to guide all living beings to fully accomplish the Buddha Way. The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha says:
"The true nature of all phenomena, ultimately empty and quiescent, is precisely the Buddha Way."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom,
Volume Five, says:
"Apart from the true nature of all phenomena, all the remaining phenomena are called Mara."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom,
Volume Ten, says:
"The Buddhas of the three times all take the true nature of all phenomena as their teacher."
In the Lotus Sutra, the World-Honored One reveals: the three vehicles are skillful means, the one vehicle is real. The Lotus Sutra,
Chapter on Skillful Means, says:
"In the buddha lands of the ten directions, there is only the one vehicle Dharma; there is no second
(referring to the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles)
and no third
(referring to the shravaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva vehicles)

, except as spoken by the Buddha as skillful means." "All Buddhas and Tathagatas, by the power of skillful means, within the one buddha vehicle distinguish and speak of three." "Only this one matter is real; the other two are not true."

The three vehicles are the lesser vehicle (that is, the shravaka vehicle), the middle vehicle (that is, the pratyekabuddha vehicle), and the great vehicle (that is, the bodhisattva vehicle). The one vehicle is also called the one buddha vehicle; it is the only teaching that can lead people to Buddhahood. The shravaka vehicle cultivates according to the Four Noble Truths and escapes birth and death; the pratyekabuddha vehicle cultivates according to the twelve links of dependent origination and escapes birth and death; the bodhisattva vehicle cultivates according to the six perfections and escapes birth and death; whereas the one buddha vehicle cultivates according to the true nature of all phenomena and perfectly accomplishes the Buddha Way.

In the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha, the World-Honored One gives very detailed instructions on what the true nature of all phenomena is, on how the true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and on how to cultivate according to the true nature of all phenomena. Master Zhiyu's
Paraphrase of the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha
provides an excellent commentary on this sutra.

blocks.text: 3. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the Supreme Meaning

inline.s: The true nature of all phenomena is the supreme meaning. The Buddha says:

"All phenomena are false; wherever they cease, that is called real, that is called true reality, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate knowledge, that is called the supreme meaning, that is called supreme emptiness."
(The Mahaparinirvana Sutra,
Volume Forty)
[Supreme meaning] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth.
The Buddha says:
"All phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like shadows, like mirages."
(The Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in a Small Compass,
Volume Ten,
Chapter Twenty-Seven on Sadaprarudita)
The Buddha says:
"Knowing that all phenomena are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root."
(The Sutra of Holding the World,
Chapter Three on the Eighteen Natures)
The Buddha says:

"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person in a night dream sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
, he sees nothing at all."
(The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit)
The Buddha says:
"Here no phenomenon arises, nor is there any phenomenon that ceases; without arising and without ceasing -- this is the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Jewel Heap Sutra,
Volume Seventy-Seven)
The Buddha says:
"The great bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as without exception empty; this is to be awakened to and know the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Five Hundred Thirty-Seven)

blocks.text: 4. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the One Dharma Seal

inline.s: The dharma seal is the seal of the Buddhadharma; it is the seal of truth handed down from Buddha to Buddha, the criterion of the Buddhadharma. Whatever does not accord with the dharma seal is not the Buddhadharma. The lesser vehicle is sealed by the "three dharma seals." The three dharma seals are: the seal of the impermanence of all conditioned things, the seal of the non-self of all phenomena, and the seal of the quiescence of nirvana. The impermanence of all conditioned things means that all things in the world are at every moment in the process of arising, dwelling, changing, and ceasing; what existed in the past has now changed, and what exists now will in the end be illusory and destroyed. The non-self of all phenomena means that all phenomena have no substantial reality. The quiescence of nirvana means that the state of nirvana extinguishes all the suffering of birth and death and is unconditioned peace and bliss; hence nirvana is quiescent.

The great vehicle is sealed by the "seal of true reality," which is also called the seal of the true nature of all phenomena. Since the true nature of all phenomena already encompasses the impermanence of all conditioned things, the non-self of all phenomena, and the quiescence of nirvana, it is called the one dharma seal or the one seal of true reality. The great vehicle takes the exposition of the principle of the true nature of all phenomena as its foundation; to speak the Dharma apart from the true nature of all phenomena is all Mara's teaching. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:
"I adorn my body with the marks, my light illumines the world; revered by countless multitudes, I proclaim the seal of true reality."
The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says:

"For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."
Master Zhiyi's Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra says:

"As for the lesser-vehicle sutras, if they bear the seal of the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvana, then they are the Buddha's teaching, and one who cultivates them attains the Way; if they lack the three dharma seals, then they are Mara's teaching. A Mahayana sutra has only one dharma seal, namely the true nature of all phenomena; it is called a sutra of definitive meaning and can lead one to the great Way. If it lacks the seal of true reality, it is Mara's teaching."
In his Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra he further says:

"The Buddhas awaken to the mark of true suchness and, riding this way of truth, appear in the world in response. They cause living beings to attain this true reality; it is solely for this matter that they appear in the world in response, and never for any other matter. Apart from the true nature of all phenomena, everything is called a matter of Mara."

In the sutras and treatises the phrase "neither arising nor ceasing" is often seen, yet it has two utterly different meanings. First, what outsiders mean by "neither arising nor ceasing" is: it has existed from the very beginning and is eternally indestructible. Second, what the Buddhadharma means by "neither arising nor ceasing" is: all things are illusory, and have never existed at all ("originally there is not a single thing"); since nothing has arisen, nothing ceases. The Buddha says:
"Here no phenomenon arises, nor is there any phenomenon that ceases; without arising and without ceasing -- this is the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Jewel Heap Sutra, Volume Seventy-Seven)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch gave a penetrating instruction on the Buddhadharma's meaning of neither arising nor ceasing:
"Jian said: You say neither arising nor ceasing -- how does this differ from the outsiders? The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)

said: What the outsiders call neither arising nor ceasing is to use ceasing to stop arising and to use arising to reveal ceasing; then ceasing is still not ceasing, and arising is said to be non-arising. What I call neither arising nor ceasing is that originally there is no arising, and now there is likewise no ceasing; therefore it is different from the outsiders."

(Translation: Xue Jian said: Master, you say neither arising nor ceasing -- how does this differ from the outsiders? The Sixth Patriarch said: What the outsiders call neither arising nor ceasing is to use ceasing to put an end to arising and to use arising to manifest ceasing; in that case ceasing is like not ceasing, and arising is, so to speak, still non-arising. But what I call neither arising nor ceasing is that it was never there from the first ("originally there is not a single thing"), and therefore there is also no ceasing; hence it differs from the outsiders.)

What the Buddhadharma means by neither arising nor ceasing is this: all phenomena have never existed (they never arose, and therefore also do not cease) -- and this is the true nature of all phenomena (the actual state of affairs of all phenomena). The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha,
Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, says:
"What is called the true nature of all phenomena? It is that all phenomena are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever."
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"All living beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death."
The Sutra of the Supreme King says:
"The unborn is real, the born is delusive. The foolish, drifting and drowning in birth and death; the Tathagata, realizing the real, is without delusion, and this is called nirvana."
The Sutra of the Humane King says:
"All phenomena, in nature truly empty, neither come nor go, neither arise nor cease; they are identical with the ultimate reality and equal to the nature of phenomena."
In the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Two Hundred Ninety-Six, the Buddha says:
"Subhuti
(Subhuti)

, in such a great treasure store of prajnaparamita, not the slightest phenomenon is spoken of as arising or ceasing, as defiled or pure, as grasped or abandoned. Why is this? Because not the slightest phenomenon can arise or cease, can be defiled or purified, can be grasped or abandoned."
The Heart Sutra says:
"All phenomena are empty in mark, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing."

Therefore, what the Buddhadharma means by neither arising nor ceasing is the true nature of all phenomena; originally there is not a single thing, so how could there be any arising or ceasing to speak of? The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra,
Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion, says:

"The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does an illusion have defilement or purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! What do you think? Does an illusion have arising or ceasing? No, World-Honored One."
Question: Why is it said that "all phenomena are illusions"?

Answer: Because all living beings are within the dream of ignorance, and all phenomena are matters within the dream of ignorance. All the myriad things of the universe are hallucinations produced when a single deluded movement of thought loses the original nature. Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way says:
"Within the dream, the six realms are clearly there; after awakening, all is empty and the great chiliocosm is gone."
(Within the dream of ignorance the six realms of rebirth are clearly there; when the dream of ignorance is awakened, all is limpid and quiescent, and the great chiliocosm simply does not exist.)
The Sutra of the Secret Adornment of the Great Vehicle says:
"Like forms in a dream
(sensory forms -- referring to visible things)
, seen only through delusive thought; once awake, they do not exist
(nonexistent once the dream is over)
Within the dream of ignorance
one sees the various forms of men and women and so on; upon attaining perfect enlightenment
(attaining Buddhahood)
one sees nothing at all."

[Perfect enlightenment] True awakening; attaining Buddhahood is called attaining perfect enlightenment. [Upon attaining perfect enlightenment one sees nothing at all] Living beings, amid the limpid and unborn, see only arising and ceasing; the Buddhas, amid what is clearly arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the World-Honored One instructs that living beings are within the dream of ignorance:

"What is ignorance? Good sons! All living beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky is truly without flowers; the diseased one falsely grasps them, and because of this false grasping he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance. Good sons! This ignorance is not a real entity,
like a person in a dream

; while dreaming he is not nonexistent, but when he awakens he attains nothing at all. Like the flowers in the sky, which cease within the sky, one cannot say they have a fixed place of ceasing. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All living beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death."

[Four great elements] The great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All tangible matter in the world has these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called "great." The four great elements here refer to the body. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"Constantly contemplate this: my present body is a convergence of the four great elements. Hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and filth all belong to earth; spittle, tears, pus, blood, fluids, phlegm, mucus, tears, semen, and excrement and urine all belong to water; warmth belongs to fire; movement belongs to wind. When the four great elements each separate, where will this false body be?"

[Shadowy traces of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six sense faculties come into contact with the six dusts; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy traces of the six dusts -- the phantom traces of the six dusts.
The Sutra of Divining the Good and Evil Karmic Retributions says:

"If among such living beings there are those who, through the perfuming of the dharma body and its power, have thinner afflictions, can grow weary of the world, seek the path of nirvana, believe in and return to the one reality, and cultivate the six perfections and all the other factors of enlightenment, they are called bodhisattvas. If among such bodhisattvas there are those who fulfill the practice of all wholesome dharmas and are
ultimately able to leave the sleep of ignorance, they are then called Buddhas
It also says:
"Because all the practices of merit are fulfilled, one becomes a Buddha. That is to say, relying on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, one can remove all obstructions,
because the dream of ignorance
is exhausted."
The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit says:
"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person,
in a night dream
, sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
he sees nothing at all."
Master Hanshan says:

"The self-nature of living beings is equal to that of the Buddha; originally it is undefiled, and it has no mark of birth and death, coming or going. But because of the first non-awakening, they are deluded about their original self-nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all kinds of delusive thoughts arise, all kinds of inversions, creating all kinds of karma, and falsely grasping the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one's own mind, one follows delusive thoughts and turns. It is like a person sound asleep having all kinds of nightmares, all kinds of states, all kinds of terror, unbearable in their many sufferings. And when he wakes, he seeks the matters of the dream and can find them nowhere. Therefore living beings fall into the
dream of ignorance
, follow delusive thoughts and inversions, create all kinds of karma, and bring all kinds of suffering upon themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, how could any of these inverted states be found?"
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Instruction to Dong Zhiguang)

[Three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by living beings who have the two desires of sexuality and food, and it includes, from the highest, the six heavens of desire, and in the middle, humans and animals, down to hungry ghosts and hells. The realm of form is the world inhabited by living beings who are free of the two desires of sexuality and food but still have a physical body, and it includes the four dhyanas and the eighteen heavens. The realm of formlessness is the world inhabited by living beings who no longer have a physical body but abide with their mind-consciousness in profound and subtle concentration, and it includes the four formless heavens (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothing whatsoever, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of ordinary people's birth-and-death rebirth; therefore the first aim of Buddhist practitioners is to leave the three realms.
Master Hanshan says:
"The Buddha says:
all phenomena are like a dream, an illusion
. He also says: birth and death, nirvana,
are like last night's dream
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Reply to Magistrate Yuan Cangru)
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"When this bodhisattva and living beings of the final age cultivate this mind and attain accomplishment, in this there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment. Perfect enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and non-dual
(the true nature of all phenomena)
; within it, the buddha worlds of hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas, inexpressible in number, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky
(illusions)
, arising and ceasing in confusion. Neither identified with
(not dwelling in any phenomenon)
nor separate from
(not abandoning any phenomenon)
them, without bondage and without liberation; only then does one know that living beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death, nirvana,
are like last night's dream

[Quiescent and non-dual] There is nothing whatsoever, and so it is called quiescent and non-dual. [Within it] Within the true realm of perfect enlightenment that is quiescent and non-dual. [Asamkhyeya] Translated into Chinese as "incalculable," it means so many that no number can calculate them. [Birth and death, nirvana, are like last night's dream] Birth and death, nirvana are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is awakened, looking back on past events is like last night's dream.
The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Five Hundred Seventy-Six, says:
"If all sentient beings could truly and thoroughly understand
that all phenomena are like illusions

, they should originally have already realized supreme enlightenment; but because sentient beings cannot comprehend that all phenomena are like illusions, they revolve in birth and death within the various destinies."
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathagata of the Great Expanse says:
"All Tathagatas, relying on this samadhi, accomplish immeasurable great majestic power, and even realize and enter the emptiness of all phenomena
(all phenomena are illusions)

, and can manifest all kinds of sovereign deeds in all buddha lands of the ten directions. For example, suppose a person dreams of all kinds of transformations, and when he awakens, all that he saw is gone. Ordinary people are likewise: because of the
dream of ignorance

, they falsely give rise to the notion of substantial reality regarding all phenomena. The Buddhas, being awakened, are attached to nothing, and therefore can, in all worlds of the ten directions, in a single thought manifest immeasurable buddha deeds, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing all living beings to accomplishment, causing them all to awaken and enter the immeasurable, profound, and wonderful gates of liberation."

All the sutras and treatises above are saying: living beings are deluded within the dream of ignorance, inverting and revolving; whereas the Buddhas have exhausted the dream of ignorance, are sovereign in regard to phenomena, and throughout the worlds of the ten directions manifest all kinds of buddha deeds to liberate living beings.
Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Reply to Magistrate Yuan Cangru, also says:
"Through the cultivation of bodhisattvas, even up to the seventh ground, they have not yet broken
the dream of ignorance

. Their teaching of living beings throughout and their accomplishment of pure lands are all buddha deeds within a dream. Therefore bodhisattvas of the eighth ground are like one crossing a river in a dream, still not abiding in awakening; only upon reaching Buddhahood is one called greatly awakened. This is stated clearly and fully recorded in the Avatamsaka Sutra, a plain and evident proof."
